## Introduction

Imputation accuracy and preservation of statistical structure are different
objectives. This vignette reuses `makeMissing()`, `evaluation()` and `nrmse()`
from [Benchmarking imputation methods](vimpute-benchmark.html), rather than
implementing another missingness generator or duplicating the core error
metrics. This reproducible benchmark compares three trained transformer
interfaces and three pretrained foundation adapters in VIM with
nearest-neighbour, random-forest and gradient-boosting imputation on two mixed-type datasets. Results below are **computed results**,
not expectations about which method should win. This vignette reads bundled
summaries: it neither downloads data nor initializes Python nor trains models
when the package is built or checked.

The default regeneration experiment uses `r paste(config$n, collapse = ", ")` rows per dataset and
`r config$repetitions` repetitions, with MCAR and MAR at 10%, 20% and 40%
missingness in **each of two selected columns**, not across the whole
table. All original predictor columns are retained. Small samples and limited
training make this a demonstration, not a definitive method ranking.

The bundled foundation comparison covers **all five row counts**, at
**`r paste(100 * foundation_rates, collapse = ", ")`% missingness**, with three
repetitions of both MCAR and MAR on both datasets.
This requests `r foundation_requested` method/scenario attempts. The bundled
snapshot includes **`r sum(runs$method %in% foundation_methods)` completed attempts**;
**`r foundation_requested - sum(runs$method %in% foundation_methods)` remain pending**.
Only completed attempts contribute to scores and plots. TabImpute's mixed-data
inference is expensive even without training; it uses the Mac GPU in this run,
while TabICL and TabPFN use CPU. The other eight methods retain the full five-size,
three-rate grid. Coverage labels distinguish pending requested runs from rates
outside the saved experiment's scope. Neither is a failed run or a zero error.

## Transformer interfaces and training

`transformerImpute(data, target, ...)` fits a new model unless `model` is supplied.
It predicts one target per call. Numeric values are represented by digit tokens;
categories by tokens. Training uses observed target rows, with an internal
80/20 training/validation split and early stopping. Numeric decoding and
categorical token sampling differ: the latter need not maximize classification
accuracy. Predictors with missing values and categories unseen among observed
target rows can lose token positions in the current encoder. This is a
limitation of this implementation, especially with rare categories.

We set `cat_vars` explicitly from factors, rather than using the default
low-cardinality heuristic, which can mistake integers for categories. These
datasets have integer-valued numeric variables, so `decimal_points = 0` and
`decimal_points_target = 0` preserve their precision. `pooling = "masked"` and
`head_dim = "compact"` use valid-position pooling and smaller attention heads.
Other settings are documented in the configuration below. They are fixed
before evaluating held-out values; no tuning uses benchmark truth.

The experimental `fit_tabular_transformer()` uses numeric value/missingness
channels and categorical embeddings with a direct regression or classification
head. We fit one model per target and apply `predict()`. The experimental
`fit_shared_transformer()` jointly learns the selected targets using masked-cell
training and one shared encoder. Both have an internal validation partition;
numeric scaling is fitted on training rows. Neither is a pretrained foundation
model. Reusable token models are also available via `fit_transformer()`,
`save_transformer()` and `load_transformer()`. We deliberately refit for every
scenario; reusing a model trained on another mask could reveal held-out values.

These interfaces require R **keras**, **tensorflow** and **reticulate**, plus a
compatible Python TensorFlow/legacy Keras environment. Numeric and unordered
factor columns are used here. Dates, arbitrary objects, hierarchical categories,
multiple imputation and out-of-sample generalization are outside this experiment.
The foundation adapters `tabimpute`, `tabiclImpute`, and `tabpfnImpute`
use pretrained PyTorch checkpoints. They are evaluated in a separate Python
environment and fresh R process, using the same incomplete tables and masks.
They condition on the observed data without training a new transformer from
scratch. Checkpoint pretraining data and budgets differ from the small neural
models above, so this compares practical imputers rather than equal training
resources. We have not independently audited upstream pretraining data for
overlap with Adult or Bank. The artificial masks protect this experiment from
using hidden target values, but do not establish independence from pretraining
data.

A mixed-data pilot exposed an embedding-size bug: deleting the target NA token
left nonconsecutive IDs, but the embedding was sized by token count. The size
now uses the largest ID plus one. A regression test covers an incomplete
categorical predictor. This is the only imputation functionality changed for
this benchmark; the reported experiment uses the corrected implementation.

## Datasets and preprocessing

* [Adult / Census Income](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/2/adult),
  Becker and Kohavi (1996), [DOI:10.24432/C5XW20](https://doi.org/10.24432/C5XW20):
  combine `adult.data` and `adult.test` (48,842 rows). Skip the test-file header,
  trim whitespace, remove the final period from test income labels, and parse
  `?` as missing. Combining the published splits is intentional: this is
  transductive reconstruction of missing cells, not a supervised income test.
* [Bank Marketing](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/222/bank+marketing),
  Moro, Rita and Cortez (2014), [DOI:10.24432/C5K306](https://doi.org/10.24432/C5K306):
  use `bank-full.csv` (45,211 rows), not the smaller sample or the different
  `bank-additional-full.csv`. Keep `unknown` as an observed category. It encodes
  recorded lack of knowledge; equating it with an artificially deleted value
  would change the evaluation target. Keep `pdays = -1` (no prior contact) as
  a structural sentinel in its original numeric column. Do not interpret it
  as a literal negative duration.

Both UCI datasets are distributed under CC BY 4.0. The script stores archive
URLs and MD5 checksums for provenance. Raw records are downloaded only with
explicit `download = TRUE` and are not bundled with VIM.

All character columns become unordered factors and all numeric measurements
remain numeric. No clipping, logarithms, balancing, rare-level pooling or
one-hot conversion is applied in shared preprocessing. Adult's `fnlwgt` remains
a predictor, not a survey weight; these are unweighted sample diagnostics.
Both education representations are retained. Bank's call duration is retained:
it is available for retrospective imputation, but would be inappropriate in a
pre-call subscription prediction task.

Remove rows with any existing NA to obtain complete references. Consequently,
Adult results describe its complete-case population and need not transfer to
people with naturally missing occupation or workclass. No correctness claim
is made for the unobserved true values in those removed rows.

```{r preprocessing, echo=FALSE}
audit <- read.csv(file.path(result_dir, "preprocessing.csv"))
knitr::kable(unique(audit[c("dataset", "rows", "complete_rows")]),
             caption = "Rows before and after complete-case selection")
knitr::kable(audit[audit$existing_na > 0 | audit$unknown > 0,
                   c("dataset", "variable", "existing_na", "unknown")],
             caption = "Existing missing values and retained unknown categories")
```

## Configuration and independent regeneration

The installed script defines functions without performing work on `source()`.
Choose a fresh output directory for each configuration. Use `resume = TRUE`
to continue an interrupted run with the identical configuration. Completed
sample sizes are reused, and completed scenarios are checkpointed within each size. Run the following **outside routine package checks**, after configuring the
Python environment. The default experiment takes substantially longer than
rendering this vignette. It saves full truth, sample indices, `makeMissing()` masks
and completed tables locally in `n250/artifacts.rds`, `n500/artifacts.rds`,
and the corresponding directories for the other sizes; only compact
metrics and provenance are shipped with the package.

```{r regenerate, eval=FALSE}
Sys.setenv(OMP_NUM_THREADS = "1", TF_NUM_INTRAOP_THREADS = "2",
           TF_NUM_INTEROP_THREADS = "2", TF_DETERMINISTIC_OPS = "1")
library(VIM)
source(system.file("benchmarks", "uci-transformer.R", package = "VIM"))
# Set RETICULATE_PYTHON before Python is initialized if selecting an environment.
# For the tested legacy Keras environment:
keras::py_require_legacy_keras(FALSE)
config <- uci_config()
config$n <- 250L#c(250L, 500L, 1000L, 2000L, 5000L)
# For a quick development run, use config$n <- 250L.
config$rates <- c(.1, .2, .4)
config$repetitions <- 3L
config$methods <- c("transformerImpute", "tabular", "shared", "kNN", "ranger", "ranger_seq10", "xgboost", "xgboost_seq10")
# Training parameters, e.g. config$transformer$epochs, can be changed here.
uci_run(config, cache = "uci-cache", output = "uci-results", download = TRUE)
uci_distribution_summary("uci-results")
# Resume after interruption (including reuse of completed sizes):
# uci_run(config, "uci-cache", "uci-results", download = FALSE, resume = TRUE)
# Reuse the archives offline:
# uci_run(config, cache = "uci-cache", output = "uci-results-offline", download = FALSE)
# To add an omitted method to a local run made with this same protocol:
# uci_extend("uci-results-subset", methods = "xgboost_seq10")
# Optional larger experiment (not the source of the displayed results):
# uci_run(uci_config(full = TRUE), "uci-cache", "uci-results-full", FALSE)
```

### Local foundation-model installation

The optional dependencies and weights are installed independently of package
checks. The following commands run from the package checkout with Python 3.11
and `uv` installed. The requirements file pins all transitive Python packages;
the setup script pins checkpoint revisions and records their SHA-256 hashes.
Weights and environments stay in the ignored `.local` directory and are
excluded from the R source package.

```{bash foundation-install, eval=FALSE}
uv venv .local/foundation-env --python 3.11
uv pip sync --python .local/foundation-env/bin/python   inst/benchmarks/foundation-requirements.txt
.local/foundation-env/bin/python inst/benchmarks/setup-foundation.py   --root .local --download
```

The R adapter needs `reticulate` and the current VIM package. Existing R
dependencies can be reused; select a project library with `R_LIBS_USER` if
installing VIM locally. Setup never accepts gated model terms automatically.
Omit `--download` to verify an existing local cache without network access.

After the eight-method run above, start a **fresh R process** and add the
foundation comparisons. Do not try to change Python interpreters in an R
process that has already initialized TensorFlow.

```{r foundation-regenerate, eval=FALSE}
source("inst/benchmarks/uci-transformer.R")
manifest <- uci_foundation_setup(".local", device = "mps") # "cpu" on other systems
uci_extend("uci-results", methods = c("tabimpute", "tabiclImpute", "tabpfnImpute"),
           rates = .2)
# To request all three missingness rates instead, omit rates in that call.
# Choose the scope before extending; use a fresh baseline copy for a new scope.
# Every completed method/scenario is checkpointed; rerun the same call after
# an interruption to reuse those completed computations.
# On a compatible Mac, device = "mps" selects the GPU for TabImpute only.
```

`uci_config(foundation = TRUE)` lists all eleven methods. The split-session
workflow avoids mixing the legacy TensorFlow environment with the pinned
foundation environment. All benchmark inference uses local checkpoints with
downloads disabled. TabPFN's explicit CPU large-dataset option is enabled by
the setup helper so that the 2,000- and 5,000-row cases can run.


```{r configuration, echo=FALSE}
str(config)
```

For the recorded run, `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`, `TF_NUM_INTRAOP_THREADS=2`,
`TF_NUM_INTEROP_THREADS=2` and `TF_DETERMINISTIC_OPS=1` were set before starting R.
The script records distinct sample, mask (`seed`) and model (`model_seed`)
seeds. Model seeds use a separate deterministic offset from mask seeds:
reusing the same seed for fixed-count MCAR sampling and a validation split
can select exactly the same rows, leaving no validation labels. All methods
receive the same model seed within a scenario. The script seeds R and
Python/NumPy/TensorFlow/Keras, clears Keras sessions
between methods, and records versions and thread settings. Exact floating-point
results and timing can still differ across hardware or library versions.

## Missingness simulation

Each repetition draws a new simple random sample without replacement from each
complete-case dataset at each of **250, 500, 1,000, 2,000 and 5,000 rows**.
The seed schedule is shared across sizes, so samples overlap and sample-size
comparisons are not independent replications. The sampling algorithm may change
with the requested size; exact nesting is not assumed. All methods share the
same sample and mask within each dataset/size/repetition/mechanism/rate scenario.
The column `n` records the number of rows in every result table. Seeds and
training budgets are unchanged across sizes: more rows imply more training
batches per epoch, not a fixed computation budget.
The targets are Adult `hours_per_week` and `income`, and Bank `balance` and `y`.
Other columns stay observed, including the MAR driver `age`.

`makeMissing()` selects exactly `round(rate * nrow(truth))` cells per
target, without replacement. MCAR uses uniform sampling. MAR uses
`weights = c(age = 1)` explicitly: the sampling weights are the logistic
transform of standardized observed age. These weights are **not** marginal
cell-deletion probabilities; the requested number of rows is sampled using
those relative weights. Higher age favours selection. Age is never masked,
and no target's hidden value drives another target's missingness. Using the
default MAR drivers instead could include the other incomplete numeric target,
so specifying the observed driver matters here.

The `where` attribute supplies the common mask for every competing method
and for scoring. We retain the original reference separately. With 250 rows,
the three requested rates correspond to 24, 48 and 96 masked cells in each
target. With other sample sizes the fractions may differ slightly due to
rounding. Masks are never redrawn to remove difficult cases.

```{r masks, eval=FALSE}
prepared <- uci_prepare("uci-cache", download = FALSE)
set.seed(config$seed)
truth <- prepared$data$Adult[sample(nrow(prepared$data$Adult), config$n[1L]), ]
incomplete <- makeMissing(truth, prop = .2, mechanism = "MAR",
  vars = c("hours_per_week", "income"), weights = c(age = 1), seed = config$seed)
mask <- attr(incomplete, "where")
incomplete <- droplevels(incomplete) # no levels learned solely from masked values
# truth is passed only to evaluation, never to a learner.
```

```{r realized-rates, echo=FALSE}
mask_rates <- unique(metrics[c("n", "dataset", "repetition", "mechanism", "rate",
                               "variable", "realized_rate")])
knitr::kable(aggregate(realized_rate ~ n + dataset + mechanism + rate + variable,
                       mask_rates, mean), digits = 3,
             caption = "Mean realized target-specific missing fractions")
```

## Competing methods and comparability

* **transformerImpute**: token transformer with compact attention and masked
  pooling; a separate call per target.
* **tabular**: separate direct tabular models per target.
* **shared**: one joint model with the two targets.
* **kNN**: `k = 5`, all other columns as distance variables, default range
  standardization, median numeric aggregation and categorical mode.
* **ranger**: `rangerImpute()` with 100 trees and one worker.
* **ranger_seq10**: `vimpute(method = "ranger", sequential = TRUE, nseq = 10)`
  with 100 trees and one worker. Both incomplete targets are updated in a
  joint sequential run. Ten is the maximum iteration count; the default
  `eps = 0.005` convergence rule can stop earlier. PMM and uncertainty draws
  are disabled (`pmm = FALSE`, `uncert = "none"`) to match the other tree
  comparisons; tuning is disabled.
* **xgboost**: `xgboostImpute()` with 30 boosting rounds and one worker.
* **xgboost_seq10**: `vimpute(method = "xgboost", sequential = TRUE, nseq = 10)`
  with 30 boosting rounds per fit and one worker. As with sequential ranger,
  both targets are updated jointly for at most ten iterations, with the default
  convergence rule, no PMM or uncertainty draws, and no tuning.
* **tabimpute**: the categorical TabImpute backend and its pinned
  `tabimpute_001.ckpt` weights. It one-hot encodes observed categories.
  Its internal row-chunk size is 32 with one chunk per inference batch.
  All rows and predictors are retained, but cross-row model context is limited
  to each chunk; this is a computational limitation, not a full-context model.
  A benchmark-only vectorized input builder reproduces the upstream tensors
  exactly while avoiding per-cell GPU synchronization; model weights and
  inference calculations are unchanged. Unused GPU allocations are released
  after each chunk, and garbage collection runs before each foundation call.
  A pilot without this cleanup exceeded the development machine's physical
  memory. The bundled timings use the cleanup policy throughout.
  Checkpoint construction is inside the measured call. The recorded run uses
  `device = "mps"`; this GPU runtime is not directly comparable to CPU-only
  timings of the other methods.
* **tabiclImpute**: TabICL 2.2.0's unsupervised interface, one ensemble member,
  one refinement pass, `temperature = 1e-8`, CPU, and no weight downloads.
* **tabpfnImpute**: TabPFN 6.0.0 with tabpfn-extensions 0.2.0, pinned v2
  classifier and regressor weights, one ensemble member, one conditional
  ordering, `temperature = 1e-9`, CPU, and no weight downloads.
  Numeric and categorical types are declared explicitly for both foundation
  interfaces instead of inferred from the number of distinct values.

The ranger and XGBoost formula interfaces, and sequential `vimpute()`, use
VIM's suggested mlr3 stack.
The runner checks exported function availability and records errors, including
missing dependencies, rather than silently omitting a method. The formula wrappers
name all other columns explicitly. All methods receive identical incomplete
values. Single-target calls always restart from the original incomplete table;
they do not receive the other target's completed values from earlier calls.
The tree wrappers may internally initialize missing predictors through
`vimpute()`, while kNN uses incomplete distances and neural encoders have their
own handling. The shared model can exploit joint training, and both sequential tree methods can use
updated imputations of the other target across iterations. These architectural
differences cannot be equated by merely matching a predictor list.

```{r example, eval=FALSE}
completed <- transformerImpute(incomplete, target = "hours_per_week",
  cat_vars = names(incomplete)[vapply(incomplete, is.factor, logical(1))],
  decimal_points = 0, decimal_points_target = 0,
  embedding_dim = 16, num_heads = 2, head_dim = "compact", pooling = "masked",
  feed_forward_dim = 32, dense_dim = 16, epochs = 5, patience = 3,
  batch_size = 64, learning_rate = .001, verbose = 0)
# The runner also fits/imputes income independently from 'incomplete'.
```

Internal validation is for early stopping only. No artificially hidden target
is used in training, predictor preprocessing, validation, tuning or model
selection. Fully observed predictors of masked rows are available, as is usual
for transductive imputation. Sample/reference statistics used below are for
**evaluation only**, never fed back into fitted models.

## Evaluation

The pointwise metrics reuse VIM's existing tools and score artificially
masked cells only:

* `evaluation()` supplies numeric mean squared error (`err_num`) and the
  fraction of incorrect categories (`err_cat`). We report RMSE as
  `sqrt(err_num)`, misclassification as `err_cat`, and accuracy as
  `1 - err_cat`. Because the current implementation of `evaluation()` sums
  errors over the supplied table, the runner **subsets its inputs to masked
  cells for each target** and passes an all-TRUE `where` matrix. This makes
  the scoring boundary explicit. Whole-table calls are equivalent only when
  observed values are preserved, which the runner also checks.
* `nrmse(x, y, m = mask)` supplies **NRMSE**, using the standard deviation of
  the **masked true values**, as implemented by VIM. This is the convention
  used by the companion benchmark. Fewer than two masked values or zero
  masked-reference variance gives an undefined score, recorded as NA.
* **NRMSE_ref** (`nrmse_reference` in the CSV) retains the alternative
  `RMSE / sd(full sampled reference column)` requested for this UCI
  benchmark. It is separate from VIM's masked-reference NRMSE; under MAR the
  two denominators can differ substantially. Both denominators are common
  across methods within a scenario and are used only for evaluation.
* MAE, whole-table marginal distances and relationship diagnostics supplement
  these existing tools; they are not available from `evaluation()` itself.

For example, after the single-target imputation above:

```{r scoring-tools, eval=FALSE}
take <- mask[, "hours_per_week"]
errors <- evaluation(
  truth[take, "hours_per_week", drop = FALSE],
  as.data.frame(completed)[take, "hours_per_week", drop = FALSE],
  where = matrix(TRUE, sum(take), 1L), vartypes = "numeric")
sqrt(errors$err_num) # RMSE on artificially removed cells
nrmse(truth$hours_per_week, completed$hours_per_week, m = take)
sqrt(errors$err_num) / sd(truth$hours_per_week) # NRMSE_ref
```

The runner rejects changed observed cells and missing, non-finite or
out-of-domain predictions. It does not clip extreme numeric predictions.
This is single-imputation scoring; it does not estimate uncertainty coverage
or proper multiple-imputation quality.

Whole-completed-table diagnostics serve a different purpose:

* mean and standard-deviation differences from the complete reference;
* maximum numeric empirical-CDF difference (KS distance, no hypothesis test)
  or categorical total-variation distance between marginal proportions;
* correlation with observed age, compared with the complete reference.
  For binary outcomes this is point-biserial correlation, with the second
  factor level coded one. A constant completion gives an undefined correlation.

These diagnostics can look reassuring when most cells remain observed even
if imputation error is large. They are not substitutes for masked-cell scores.
Elapsed wall time includes fitting and prediction of both targets, internal
validation and initialization; it excludes download, preprocessing and result
writing, but includes scoring. It is measured once per method/scenario, not
summed over duplicated per-target rows. The original core run randomizes method order within
scenarios; later extensions use their declared method order. There is no hardware-normalized speed or peak-memory claim.
At 250 rows, the original seven methods, including sequential ranger, were run together using
the `makeMissing()` masks. Sequential XGBoost was subsequently added with
`uci_extend()`, reusing the exact saved samples, masks and model seeds. Its
runtime was measured in a separate session, so timing comparisons also reflect
between-session variation. The larger sizes ran the original eight methods together,
with the same parameters. Foundation methods were added in separate sessions
using the saved samples, masks and seeds; their environment and device settings
are recorded with the results. Earlier results from the custom Bernoulli generator
are not mixed into these tables. Random seeds reproduce this protocol, but
using the same seed with a different generator does not reproduce old masks.

## Results

The saved run contains `r nrow(runs)` method/scenario attempts,
`r sum(runs$status == "ok")` successful completions and
`r sum(runs$status != "ok")` recorded failures. Every method in a scenario
uses the same `makeMissing()` mask.

```{r status, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(table(runs$n, runs$dataset, runs$method, runs$status)),
             col.names = c("Rows", "Dataset", "Method", "Status", "Runs"))
failed <- runs[runs$status != "ok", c("n", "dataset", "repetition", "mechanism", "rate", "method", "error")]
if (nrow(failed)) knitr::kable(failed)
```

The following tables retain number of rows, dataset, mechanism and nominal rate. Scores are
means across successful repetitions, with their sample standard deviations in
parentheses. Counts are shown so failures cannot improve a ranking invisibly.
With three repetitions, standard deviations describe variation only roughly;
they are not confidence intervals or significance tests. Methods are paired by
sample and mask, so formal comparisons would require paired analysis and more
repetitions. Empty cells indicate unavailable metrics. Success counts use completed
attempts as the denominator. The Coverage column distinguishes pending requested
repetitions from scenarios outside the saved foundation grid.

```{r result-tables, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
fmt <- function(x) {
  x <- x[is.finite(x)]
  if (!length(x)) return("—")
  sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", mean(x), if (length(x) > 1) sd(x) else NA_real_)
}
for (nr in config$n) for (ds in unique(runs$dataset)) for (mech in unique(runs$mechanism)) {
  cat("\n\n### ", ds, ": ", mech, ", ", nr, " rows\n\n", sep = "")
  tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(config$rates, function(rate) {
    do.call(rbind, lapply(config$methods, function(method) {
      x <- metrics[metrics$n == nr & metrics$dataset == ds & metrics$mechanism == mech &
                     metrics$rate == rate & metrics$method == method, ]
      rr <- runs[runs$n == nr & runs$dataset == ds & runs$mechanism == mech &
                   runs$rate == rate & runs$method == method, ]
      requested <- if (method %in% foundation_methods && !rate %in% foundation_rates) 0L else config$repetitions
      pending <- max(0L, requested - nrow(rr))
      data.frame(Rate = rate, Method = method,
        Coverage = if (!requested) "Not requested" else if (pending)
          paste(pending, "pending") else "Complete",
        Success = paste(sum(rr$status == "ok"), nrow(rr), sep = "/"),
        RMSE = fmt(x$rmse), MAE = fmt(x$mae), NRMSE = fmt(x$nrmse), NRMSE_ref = fmt(x$nrmse_reference),
        Accuracy = fmt(x$accuracy), Misclassification = fmt(x$misclassification),
        Seconds = fmt(rr$elapsed[rr$status == "ok"]))
    }))
  }))
  print(knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE))
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

```{r error-plot, echo=FALSE, eval=has_ggplot, fig.height=12}
library(ggplot2)
numeric_scores <- subset(metrics, type == "numeric")
ggplot(numeric_scores, aes(factor(rate), nrmse, colour = method, group = method)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line",
    data = function(d) if (length(foundation_rates) > 1L) d else
      d[!d$method %in% foundation_methods, ]) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = .25), alpha = .65) +
  facet_grid(n + dataset ~ mechanism, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = "log1p") +
  labs(x = "Nominal missing fraction", y = "VIM masked-reference NRMSE (log1p scale)",
       colour = "Method", caption = "Points: repetitions; lines: means. Lower is better.") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r categorical-plot, echo=FALSE, eval=has_ggplot, fig.height=12}
ggplot(subset(metrics, type == "categorical"),
       aes(factor(rate), accuracy, colour = method, group = method)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line",
    data = function(d) if (length(foundation_rates) > 1L) d else
      d[!d$method %in% foundation_methods, ]) +

  theme_minimal()
```

## Discussion and limitations

The token encoder constructs/drops token positions separately for training
and prediction. This can produce incompatible sequence widths or lose
positions for rare or unseen categories. Any failures in the current run are
listed above; they are not repaired by silently changing masks or predictors.
A failed two-target run contributes no pointwise scores for either target,
even if one target finished first. The per-scenario success counts show its
impact. The paired summary below excludes an entire scenario from all methods
if any competitor fails.

Interpret the results in the context of small, unbalanced samples: accuracy on
income/subscription can be high by predicting the majority class. Categorical
sampling may preserve a marginal distribution while reducing exact-match
accuracy. Conversely, conditional-mean regression can score well on RMSE while
shrinking variance. Bank balances are skewed; a few large errors can dominate
RMSE. There is no imputation-range constraint on numeric token decoding.

Five training epochs are a limited budget, not a claim of convergence. Direct
and shared transformers encode numbers more naturally than digit prediction,
but they still learn from scratch. Early stopping, per-target training and
Python initialization affect runtime. Equal epoch counts do not imply equal
work or equal tuning quality across architectures. A larger sample, more
repetitions, separate tuning data and a predeclared training budget are needed
before choosing a method for production. Sparse or very high-cardinality
categorical targets, missingness in all predictors, other MAR drivers and MNAR
are not established by this experiment.

The per-scenario tables and plots above use each method's successful runs.
The first paired summary retains scenarios completed by all eight original
methods. The second retains the set attempted and completed by
all eleven methods. These separate comparisons preserve the full sample-size
study without treating unrequested foundation runs as failures.

```{r findings, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
scenario_key <- function(d) paste(d$n, d$dataset, d$repetition, d$mechanism, d$rate)
paired_summary <- function(methods, label) {
  selected_runs <- runs[runs$method %in% methods, ]
  all_ok <- vapply(split(selected_runs, scenario_key(selected_runs)), function(z)
    length(unique(z$method)) == length(methods) &&
      nrow(z) == length(methods) && all(z$status == "ok"), logical(1))
  common <- names(all_ok)[all_ok]
  if (!length(common)) {
    cat(label, ": no common successful scenarios.\n")
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  paired_metrics <- metrics[metrics$method %in% methods &
                              scenario_key(metrics) %in% common, ]
  paired_runs <- selected_runs[scenario_key(selected_runs) %in% common, ]
  findings <- merge(
    aggregate(nrmse ~ n + dataset + method, paired_metrics, mean),
    aggregate(accuracy ~ n + dataset + method, paired_metrics, mean))
  findings <- merge(findings, aggregate(elapsed ~ n + dataset + method, paired_runs, median))
  print(knitr::kable(findings, digits = 3,
    caption = paste(label, "on", length(common),
                    "common successful scenarios; median runtime in seconds")))
}
paired_summary(setdiff(config$methods, foundation_methods), "Original methods")
if (any(config$methods %in% foundation_methods))
  paired_summary(config$methods, "Including foundation methods")
```

```{r foundation-findings, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
for (dataset in c("Adult", "Bank")) {
  selected <- metrics[metrics$n == max(config$n) & metrics$dataset == dataset &
                        metrics$rate == .2 & metrics$method %in% foundation_methods, ]
  if (!nrow(selected)) next
  summary <- merge(aggregate(nrmse ~ method, selected, mean),
                   aggregate(accuracy ~ method, selected, mean))
  if (nrow(summary) != length(foundation_methods)) next
  numeric_best <- summary[which.min(summary$nrmse), ]
  categorical_best <- summary[which.max(summary$accuracy), ]
  cat(sprintf(paste0("For **%s** at %s rows and 20%% missingness, among the three ",
    "pretrained adapters, **%s** has the lowest mean numerical NRMSE (%.3f), ",
    "and **%s** has the highest mean categorical accuracy (%.1f%%), averaged ",
    "over the MCAR and MAR repetitions. These are descriptive comparisons ",
    "under the stated inference budgets, not evidence of general superiority.\n\n"),
    dataset, format(max(config$n), big.mark = ","), numeric_best$method,
    numeric_best$nrmse, categorical_best$method, 100 * categorical_best$accuracy))
}
```

In the bundled five-epoch run, all three transformers trained from scratch have lower mean
numeric NRMSE and higher categorical accuracy at 5,000 rows than at 250 rows
on both datasets. This endpoint comparison does not imply a monotonic
improvement at every intermediate size. At 5,000 rows, the direct tabular model
and sequential XGBoost have similar mean numeric NRMSE on Bank; the token
transformer still has higher numeric error and lower categorical accuracy than
all five established baselines on both datasets. Runtime rankings also change:
the shared transformer is faster than kNN at 5,000 rows, although both ranger
and XGBoost variants remain faster than the shared transformer.

The paired summary separates sample sizes. Compare accuracy and runtime together:
additional rows increase the information available to learners but also the
number of training batches and distance calculations. A lower error at a larger
size is descriptive evidence for these samples, not proof of a general learning
curve. The three repetitions and overlapping samples limit precision. Neither
the mean error nor a single dataset establishes transformer superiority.

## Reproducibility information

The installed `benchmarks/uci-results` directory contains `metrics.csv`
(per target), `runs.csv` (including failures and warnings), `config.rds`,
`preprocessing.csv`, `sources.csv`, `distributions.csv`, and
per-size environment records combined in `session.txt`. The 250-row records
include the original seven-method run and the sequential XGBoost addition.
Larger-size records describe their own sessions. The full regeneration
artifact is intentionally kept outside the package. To update the vignette,
rerun the script and replace these compact files together; do not hand-edit
numbers. The test suite checks mask reproducibility, MAR's dependence only on
observed age, VIM's masked-reference and full-reference scoring denominators, unchanged observed cells and offline
behaviour without invoking TensorFlow.

```{r source-checksums, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(read.csv(file.path(result_dir, "sources.csv")))
```
